description: Renovate owns dependency updates for this repository because Dependabot cannot.
GitHub lists Bun as supported for version updates but NOT for security updates, so the
config-free security-update path falls back to the npm_and_yarn updater, which cannot read
bun.lock and fails with dependency_file_not_supported. No .github/dependabot.yml fixes that;
there is no ecosystem entry that unlocks Dependabot security updates for Bun. Renovate has a
dedicated bun manager instead, which reads the text bun.lock and the packages/* workspaces.
Operator coupling worth knowing before changing repository settings: leave Dependabot ALERTS
and the dependency graph ENABLED even though Dependabot SECURITY UPDATES are turned off.
vulnerabilityAlerts reads GitHub's alert feed, so turning alerts off costs that input. It is
not the only one - osvVulnerabilityAlerts below queries a local OSV database and never calls
GitHub - so the two are complementary rather than one being indispensable.
baseBranchPatterns is a product-history guard, not a style preference. Archon was rewritten
(#957) and the Python-era product was archived rather than deleted. It still lives on
archive/v1-stable and archive/v1-task-management-rag, which carry python/pyproject.toml,
archon-ui-main/package.json and their own Dockerfiles - manifests of a product that no longer
exists. Naming the working branch is what keeps Renovate off them; leaving the key out would
make that depend on the repository's default-branch setting instead.
Off by Renovate default, and the reason this file exists. Most of this repository's exposure
is not a declared range that is too old - it is a range that already permits a patched
version while the frozen bun.lock resolves to a stale one. That class produces no GitHub
alert at all, because the range *could* resolve to something patched, so no alert-driven
automation finds it however it is configured. Regenerating the lockfile does, and deleting
bun.lock then running bun install is exactly what Renovate's bun manager does here.
It also reaches the transitive packages: nothing declares them, so they can never be the
subject of a per-package PR - they move only when their parents move.
An override reaches the installed tree WITHOUT passing the range check that governs every
other route, so a major bump here can force a dependent onto a version its own declared
range forbids, and bun install --frozen-lockfile still succeeds. That bypass is live at
this commit: msw@2.12.10 declares path-to-regexp ^6.3.0 while the override resolves 8.4.2,
two majors outside it, with no error. Until now every line in this block was a deliberate
human act with an advisory behind it; Renovate now writes here too.
So majors in overrides are a human decision. Patch and minor still flow, which is the
whole class this file exists to automate - the axios, qs and @hono/node-server refreshes
landed in this PR were all in-range patch moves.
